4f6e0c34a2.q: What is the correct positioning for the upper extremity flexor synergy pattern in a stroke patient with right-sided hemiparesis?
4f6e0c34a2.a: For a patient presenting with upper extremity flexor synergy pattern after stroke, the most appropriate resting position is forearm pronation. This positioning opposes the flexor synergy component of forearm supination, helping move the patient out of synergy and reducing the risk of contractures and loss of range of motion.

ec117718d2.q: Why is shoulder abduction incorrect as a resting position for a patient with flexor synergy after left middle cerebral artery stroke?
ec117718d2.a: Shoulder abduction is part of the upper extremity flexor synergy pattern itself, so positioning a patient in shoulder abduction reinforces the existing abnormal movement pattern. The NPTE asks clinicians to move patients out of synergy, not reinforce it, even though a movement might sound therapeutically reasonable.

f: Middle cerebral artery strokes impact the upper extremity more than the lower extremity. A left middle cerebral artery stroke causes contralateral body issues, resulting in right-sided hemiparesis. When a patient sustains this type of stroke, they typically present with a flexor synergy pattern in the upper extremity, which includes specific abnormal movement patterns. The flexor synergy pattern comprises scapular retraction and elevation, shoulder abduction and external rotation, elbow flexion, forearm supination, and wrist and finger flexion.

For positioning interventions in patients with this presentation, the goal is to move the patient out of the existing synergy pattern to reduce the risk of contractures and loss of range of motion. This means positioning the affected upper extremity in ways that oppose the components of the flexor synergy pattern. For example, if the patient presents with forearm supination as part of the flexor synergy, positioning the forearm in pronation helps counteract that component. The same principle applies to other joints involved in the synergy—moving toward extension when the synergy produces flexion, and toward positions opposite to those reinforced by the abnormal pattern.
